headline: Canada Factory Sales Recover in August With Increased Prices

paragraphs.text: OTTAWA--Canadian manufacturing activity picked up in August on the back of higher prices and with record metal sales for the month.
Factory shipments increased 1.5% from the month before to a seasonally adjusted 79.88 billion Canadian dollars, the equivalent of about US$56.1 billion, Statistics Canada said Thursday.

The advance, which was stronger than the data agency's advance estimate sales were up 1.1%, marked a sixth rise in factory trade in the last seven months following a 0.3% dip in July. Still, the volume of sales in August was little changed as prices measured by the industrial product price index climbed 1.3%.

Sales by Canada's wholesalers, who make up the largest component of the country's services sector, dropped by 1.6% between July and August to C$91.58 billion and fell by a sharper 1.8% in volume terms.

The drop in sales volumes may reflect some hesitancy after President Trump in late August followed through on threats made the month before to impose fresh tariffs on Canadian goods representing about 5% of exports to the U.S. It also suggests some risk to advance data that had pointed to a rise in gross domestic product for the month, Capital Economics senior North America economist Thomas Ryan said.
"Hopes of a strong recovery in activity led by manufacturing earlier this year look to have proved premature, with newly enforced U.S. tariffs partly to blame," Ryan said.

Jobs data released last week showed that employment in manufacturing declined by 12,700 in September, the first pullback since June. Although up in 2026, manufacturing jobs have fallen by roughly 40,000 from a January 2025 peak before the first round of U.S. tariffs came into effect.

Manufacturing sales were up in 12 of the 21 industry segments tracked by Statistics Canada, led by a 14% jump in sales in the primary metal sector to C$7.6 billion, the highest level on record, thanks mainly to non-ferrous metals with strong demand for copper, silver and other metals.

Chemical sales also were up strongly, recouping weakness in July, thanks mainly to high prices. However, sales of transportation equipment were down for a second straight month with weakness in motor vehicles and parts that in part reflected an extended summer shutdown of an auto assembly plant.

New factory orders were down 0.7% from a month earlier, and unfilled orders, the stock of orders that will contribute to future sales if they aren't canceled, were flat. Manufacturing inventories increased 0.2%, continuing an upward trend since January.

The retreat in wholesale trade in August after increases the previous two months was led by a drop in sales of vehicles and parts, the first fall after six consecutive increases. Sales of agricultural supplies also fell steeply, notably potash, though trade in building materials and supplies rose an eight straight month.
Including receipts from petroleum, oilseed and grain merchants, wholesale sales for August fell 1% from the month before, while inventories on the same basis nudged up 0.2%.

Statistics Canada previously estimated the economy was growing again in August, with advance data pointing to a 0.2% rise in industry-level gross domestic product from the month before, thanks to a recovery in mining and retail trade that offset further declines in oil and gas extraction. GDP in July was steady, snapping three straight months of expansion.
